html:
A design question that tests queues, retries and good manners:

Many services in your company need to notify users: "Your order has shipped", "New login from Chrome", "Sale starts now". Design one system that sends push, email and SMS for all of them. About 50 million notifications a day, with marketing bursts to 10 million users at once.

The Numbers First

  • 50 million a day is about 600 per second on average.
  • A marketing burst of 10 million in a few minutes is tens of thousands per second.
  • Providers set the real limits: push services, email providers and SMS gateways each accept only so many requests per second, and SMS costs money per message.

So the system must absorb bursts and send at the pace each provider allows.

The Naive Version

Each service calls the email or push provider directly, inside its own request:

def ship_order(order):
    mark_as_shipped(order)
    email_provider.send(order.customer.email, "Your order has shipped")

It breaks quickly:

  • A slow provider slows the order service. If the email call hangs, shipping an order hangs.
  • A failed call is lost. Nobody retries it.
  • No shared rules. Every team has to handle opt-outs, quiet hours and templates again, differently.
  • No limits. A marketing script can send a user ten messages in an hour.

The Design

Services → Notification API → Queues (push / email / SMS) → Channel workers → Providers
                 ↓
      Preferences, templates, rate limits
  1. Services call one API, with a user, a notification type and data: { userId, type: "order_shipped", data: { orderId } }.
  2. The API applies the rules: is this type enabled for this user and channel? Is it quiet hours? Has the user had too many today? Then it renders the template in the user's language.
  3. It puts one message per channel on a queue and answers right away. The calling service is done.
  4. Workers per channel read their queue and call the provider. Each attempt updates the notification's status.

The queue decouples the services from the providers: bursts wait in the queue, and a slow SMS gateway only slows SMS.

Retries Without Duplicates

Providers fail and time out. Workers retry with exponential backoff: after 1 second, then 2, 4, 8… up to a limit. After the last attempt, the message goes to a dead-letter queue for someone to look at.

A timeout is tricky: the provider may have sent the message before the connection dropped. Retrying could send it twice. Two defenses:

  • Give each notification an idempotency key and pass it to providers that support one.
  • Record what was sent, and skip a notification whose key is already marked as delivered.

Exactly-once delivery isn't possible end to end, so the goal is at least once, with deduplication for the messages that matter.

Priorities

A password reset must not wait behind 10 million sale announcements. Use separate queues, or priority levels, for:

  • Transactional messages: password resets, security alerts, receipts. Small volume, sent first.
  • Marketing messages: campaigns and newsletters. Huge volume, sent at a steady pace.

Respecting Users

  • Preferences per type and channel: someone may want order updates by push but never by SMS.
  • Quiet hours in the user's time zone, except for urgent security alerts.
  • Frequency caps: at most a few marketing messages a day.
  • Digests: group many similar events, like ten new comments, into one notification.
  • Unsubscribe links in every email, as the law requires in many countries.

Every Failure, and What Happens

What goes wrong What happens Result
Email provider is down Email workers retry with backoff Emails are delayed, push and SMS unaffected
A worker crashes mid-send The queue gives the message to another worker Possibly sent twice; the key deduplicates it
A 10-million-user burst arrives Messages wait in the marketing queue Sent over minutes; transactional ones go first
A device token has expired The push provider rejects it Remove the token; stop sending to it
A bug sends the same campaign twice The idempotency key matches the first run The repeat is skipped

Details Interviewers Ask About

  • Scheduling. "Send at 9 a.m. local time" means storing the send time per user and releasing messages into the queue when due.
  • Tracking. Record sent, delivered, opened and clicked, from provider callbacks and tracking links, to measure campaigns.
  • Templates. Keep them versioned, with a preview, so a typo in a campaign is caught before 10 million people see it.
  • Multiple providers. A second email or SMS provider gives a fallback when the first one fails.

The Answer in Short

  1. Put one notification API in front of every service, so rules live in one place.
  2. Check preferences, quiet hours and caps, then render the template.
  3. Queue one message per channel, and answer immediately.
  4. Send with workers per channel, at each provider's pace.
  5. Retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue; deduplicate with idempotency keys.
  6. Keep transactional messages ahead of marketing ones.
